passage: I'm Mariam, and I sit near the door at the travel agency, so I see who comes in when. Imran walked in at 10:25 on Tuesday, forty minutes late, rain dripping off his helmet. Usha, our manager, didn't look up. "Some people just don't take this job seriously," she said, loudly enough for him to hear. On Thursday, Usha herself came in at 10:15. "The flyover was jammed, total nightmare," she told us, and everyone nodded. I didn't say anything, but I must have glanced at Imran, because Usha followed my eyes. She went quiet. Later she called Imran in, and I heard her ask, "Tuesday, was it the rain? What's your route like?" I can't say what changed inside her. But her voice was different.

qa.q: What time did Imran walk in on Tuesday?
qa.a: Imran walked in at 10:25 on Tuesday, forty minutes late.

qa.q: What might Usha have been thinking when she went quiet?
qa.a: Usha may have felt embarrassed, realising she blamed Imran's attitude for his lateness but the flyover for her own.

qa.q: Why is Usha's question 'What's your route like?' a better start?
qa.a: It is curious rather than accusing, so Imran can explain the rain or his route, and any feedback can be fair.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt hearing 'Some people just don't take this job seriously'?
qa.a: Imran, still dripping from the rain, probably felt judged in front of everyone for something outside his control. 😔

grounding: A colleague watches a manager blame a late employee's attitude, excuse her own lateness by traffic, then notice and ask questions.

passage:
Monday. Tushar arrived at the clinic reception at 9:20, twenty minutes late. Ganga, the front-office manager, wrote in her notebook: "Tushar, careless attitude." She told him sharply that patients were waiting.
Wednesday. Ganga's scooter got a flat on the ring road and she walked in at 9:30. "Nothing I could do," she told the receptionist, annoyed at the tyre, not at herself. That evening, filling in her notebook, she saw Monday's line about Tushar and stopped. She had never asked him why.
The following Monday. Ganga called Tushar in before opening. "You were late last week. What happened?" He explained that the bus from his colony had been cancelled twice that month. They agreed he'd take the earlier bus and message her if it was cancelled. Her feedback note said exactly that.

qa.q: What did Ganga write in her notebook on Monday?
qa.a: She wrote, 'Tushar, careless attitude.'

qa.q: What made Ganga stop when she saw Monday's line?
qa.a: Having just blamed a flat tyre for her own lateness, she realised she had judged Tushar's attitude without ever asking why he was late.

qa.q: What did Ganga's new feedback note get right?
qa.a: It recorded the real cause, the cancelled bus, and a practical plan, instead of a label about attitude.

qa.q: What would change for Tushar if Ganga had never looked back at her notebook?
qa.a: He would still be marked as careless for cancelled buses and might feel he could never explain himself.

grounding: Over a week, a manager notices she blamed an employee's attitude for lateness but her own on a flat tyre, and makes her feedback fairer.

passage: Keerthana, you've mentioned Dinesh's late arrivals three times this evening. Let me tell you what happened to me, back when I was twenty-five, a young woman running my first shift at the garment unit. There was a tailor, Selvi, always ten minutes late. I decided she was lazy and told her so in front of everyone. One morning my bus broke down and I came in forty minutes late. I walked in blaming the bus, the road, the monsoon, and nobody questioned me. That evening my old supervisor, Mr Fernandes, laughed at me. "Ayesha, late you is unlucky, and late Selvi is lazy?" The next day I asked Selvi about her mornings. She dropped two children at two schools before work. We moved her shift by fifteen minutes. So first, ask Dinesh how his mornings go.

qa.q: How late was Ayesha on the morning the bus broke down?
qa.a: Ayesha came in forty minutes late.

qa.q: Why did young Ayesha decide Selvi was lazy?
qa.a: Young Ayesha felt annoyed because she only saw Selvi arrive late and never her mornings, so laziness seemed obvious, while her own lateness felt clearly the bus's fault.

qa.q: What does Ayesha want Keerthana to do about Dinesh?
qa.a: Ayesha wants Keerthana to ask Dinesh how his mornings go before judging his late arrivals.

qa.q: How might Selvi have felt being called lazy in front of everyone?
qa.a: Selvi, who was dropping two children at two schools, probably felt humiliated and unseen.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a young woman running a shift, blaming a tailor's laziness for lateness while blaming the bus for her own, and changing course.

passage:
Heavy rain had flooded half of Chennai's roads by Monday, and the call centre was short-staffed. Lokesh came in at 9:40, forty minutes late, soaked to the knees. Their manager, Revathi, didn't look up. "Some people just don't take this job seriously," she said, loud enough for the floor to hear.
Shankar, at the next desk, said nothing. He'd seen Lokesh's route on the news: the subway was underwater.
On Wednesday Revathi herself walked in at 10:05, shaking out her umbrella. "The traffic was impossible," she said. "Nobody could have made it."
Shankar waited until the lunch break. "Ma'am, on Monday it was Lokesh's subway," he said quietly. "Same rain."
Revathi paused, fork in the air. Then she went to Lokesh's desk. "Monday, you came through the flooded subway?" she asked. "What would make those days easier?" They agreed on a flood-day call-in rule.

qa.q: What time did Revathi walk in on Wednesday?
qa.a: She walked in at 10:05.

qa.q: Why did Revathi feel her own lateness was about traffic but Lokesh's was about attitude?
qa.a: She knew exactly what her own journey was like, so the rain explained her delay, but she hadn't seen Lokesh's route, so his lateness seemed to show he didn't take the job seriously.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that helped Revathi's feedback become fairer?
qa.a: He waited for a private moment and quietly linked her rain excuse to Lokesh's flooded subway, which led her to ask Lokesh what would make those days easier.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel when Revathi asks him about the subway on Wednesday?
qa.a: After being criticised in front of the floor on Monday, Lokesh would likely feel relief that the flooded route is finally being understood.

grounding: Seen by a colleague, it shows a manager blaming a late employee's attitude while blaming traffic for her own lateness, and becoming curious once the double standard is noticed.

passage:
In the Andheri office of a printing firm, Francis had come in late four times in two weeks. Each time, the design head, Deepali, frowned at the clock and said, "No discipline, that boy." She'd started leaving him off the morning planning emails.
Samir, who sat by the window, had a clear view of both the clock and the door. On Thursday Deepali arrived half an hour late herself and sighed to the room, "The local was stuck at Bandra, nothing I could do."
Samir hesitated, then asked her quietly over tea, "Does Francis take the same train?"
Deepali looked at him. "Why?"
"He comes from Virar. Longer line."
For a moment she didn't answer. Then she went over to Francis's desk. "You're often late. Is it the trains, or something else?" she asked, and for the first time she sounded like she wanted to know.

qa.q: From where does Francis come to work, according to Samir?
qa.a: He comes from Virar.

qa.q: Why did 'no discipline' feel like the right explanation to Deepali at first?
qa.a: She felt annoyed seeing Francis walk in late, but she never saw his long train journey, so his character seemed the only cause, while her own late train felt like obvious bad luck.

qa.q: What small step did Samir take, and what change did it lead to?
qa.a: He quietly asked whether Francis took the same train, which made Deepali notice the double standard and go to ask Francis what was really causing the lateness.

qa.q: How might Francis have felt about being left off the morning planning emails?
qa.a: Francis likely felt pushed aside and judged, perhaps without knowing why, and may be surprised when Deepali finally asks about the trains.

grounding: Seen by a colleague, it shows a manager blaming a late employee's attitude while excusing her own lateness by the trains, and asking with curiosity once she notices.

passage:
"Joel's late again," Rehana said, dropping her bag on her desk at 9:25. "Twenty minutes. He just doesn't take this job seriously."
Shalini looked up from her screen. "What time did you get in?"
"9:20. But the flyover was jammed; there was an accident near the signal."
"Joel takes the same flyover."
Rehana paused. "That's different. He's late a lot."
"He was late twice this month. You were late three times."
"Because of traffic!"
"Maybe his were too," Shalini said gently. "You're giving yourself the traffic and giving him the attitude."
Rehana sat down slowly. "Okay. That's annoyingly fair."
"Maybe ask him what's going on before the feedback meeting?"
"Yeah." Rehana opened her diary. "And maybe I'll ask how his commute is."

passage: In my first job at the bank branch, I sat right outside our manager's cabin, so I heard things. One morning Naveen came in fifteen minutes late, and Mrs Grewal said loudly, "Some people have no discipline." The next week she arrived forty minutes late herself and told us, "The school bus broke down, I had to drop my son." Nobody said anything. I didn't either, at first. But when she started drafting Naveen's warning letter, I asked if I could mention something. "Ma'am, Naveen's mother has dialysis on Tuesdays. He's late on Tuesdays." She put the pen down. After a while she said, "I gave myself a reason and gave him a character." She called Naveen in, asked about Tuesdays and moved his start time. Later she said, "Amandeep, thank you for saying it."

qa.q: Why was Mrs Grewal forty minutes late?
qa.a: The school bus broke down and she had to drop her son.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep speak up about Naveen's Tuesdays?
qa.a: Amandeep felt uneasy that Naveen was about to be warned for something with a real reason, while Mrs Grewal excused her own lateness.

qa.q: What did Mrs Grewal do after hearing about Tuesdays, and why is it fairer?
qa.a: She asked Naveen about Tuesdays and moved his start time, giving him the same understanding she gave herself.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel when asked about Tuesdays instead of warned?
qa.a: Naveen would probably feel relieved and respected, with his mother's care recognised.

passage:
HR partner's note, after the quarterly reviews, 12 July
In today's review, Parveen, one of our newest managers, described Anirban as having "a casual attitude" because he had arrived late to four morning meetings. Earlier in the same session, when I asked about her own two late arrivals, she had explained them as "the metro breakdowns that week." I asked her, gently, whether Anirban might have been on the same metro line. She checked: he was. She laughed at herself a little and said, "I gave myself the metro and gave him an attitude." She rewrote the comment as a question for their next one-to-one: "What's been making mornings hard?" I will suggest that all new managers check their feedback for the same pattern before submitting.

qa.q: How did Parveen explain her own late arrivals?
qa.a: The metro breakdowns that week.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel on finding Anirban used the same metro line?
qa.a: She felt a little embarrassed and laughed at herself, recognising the double standard.

qa.q: How did Parveen change her feedback, and why is it better?
qa.a: She turned the attitude comment into the question "What's been making mornings hard?", which is fair and curious.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel in the next one-to-one?
qa.a: Anirban would probably feel respected and able to explain, instead of being judged as casual.

grounding: An HR note records a new manager noticing she blamed traffic for herself but attitude for an employee, and rewriting her feedback.

passage:
Tuesday.
Hansa came in forty minutes late today, hair wet, saying the flyover was jammed after a truck broke down. Fair enough; it was on the news. Then at 11, the new trainee walked in twenty minutes late and Hansa said to him, in front of all of us, "This is about attitude. If you cared, you'd leave earlier." He said the bus hadn't come. At five I asked Hansa, gently, if the trainee's bus might have been stuck on the flyover too. She went quiet. Then she said, "You're right. I gave myself the traffic and gave him the attitude." She walked over to his desk before she left.
Sunaina

When Rakesh logged in twenty minutes late on Tuesday, Trisha muttered, "Lazy. No discipline." She wrote a warning note.

On Thursday, Trisha arrived forty minutes late. "The flyover was blocked," she said. "Complete chaos."

passage:
Dear Lakshmi,

I hope you don't mind me writing this. I've been meaning to say something since last week's team meeting.

When Pasang came in late on Tuesday, you said to the group that he "doesn't take the job seriously". On Friday, you were late yourself because of the rain and the metro delays. You mentioned the metro, and that made sense.

I think you're a really fair manager, which is why I'm raising it. It seemed like when you're late, it's the circumstances, but when Pasang is, it's his attitude.

I asked him about Tuesday. His landlord had locked him out after a water leak, and he'd spent two hours finding a key.

Maybe next time, we could ask first? I'd want someone to ask me.

Thank you for reading this.

Dolma

qa.q: Why was Lakshmi late on Friday?
qa.a: You were late yourself because of the rain and the metro delays.

qa.q: What does Dolma seem to feel about raising this with Lakshmi?
qa.a: Dolma seems nervous but respectful, wanting to be fair to Pasang while not offending Lakshmi.

qa.q: Why is Dolma's letter a helpful way to raise the double standard?
qa.a: Dolma is respectful, gives facts about both lateness cases and Pasang's reason, and suggests asking first, making feedback more curious.

qa.q: How might Pasang have felt being called someone who "doesn't take the job seriously"?
qa.a: Pasang probably felt hurt and misjudged, having spent two hours locked out.

passage: You asked what the new job's like. Okay, one story.
